Who we are

Teqball Mumbai is a high-performance teqball club and ecosystem founded by Vinit Jain in 2021, running an athlete development pathway, the Mumbai Teq League, and the training ground behind India's Asian Youth Games teqball representative, built around teqball, the football-based table sport now on the programme at major multi-sport games across Asia.

From our club to the Asian stage

In October 2025, teqball made its debut at the Asian Youth Games in Bahrain, and Teqball Mumbai's Atharva Sakpal wore India's colours and finished 9th in Men's Singles, with club founder Vinit Jain serving as Team India Coach.

More Than a Sport

Teqball sharpens the first touch, control and decision-making that footballers rely on, which is why Teqball Mumbai's ecosystem crosses over with professional football, through partners including Mumbai City FC and All Stars FC.

Mumbai Teq League

Now in its 7th season, the Mumbai Teq League has brought 300+ athletes through its ranks. Season 7 has just concluded with 48 players competing.

About

What Teqball Mumbai is, why it exists, and where it's going.

Our story

Teqball Mumbai was founded by Vinit Jain in 2021, two years after he became the first Indian to win an international Teqball match, at the 2019 Asian-Pacific Teqball Cup in China. The full origin story, in Vinit's own words, is still to come.

Mission
  • Develop athletes: capable of competing at international standards, from grassroots to elite level.
  • Create opportunities: competitive pathways through district, national and international competitions.
  • Build a sustainable ecosystem: club, league, sponsors and community working as one.
  • Represent India internationally: putting Indian athletes on Asian and world stages.
  • Grow the grassroots: bringing teqball to schools, colleges and new communities.

The Journey

2019
Vinit Jain wins Gold in Men's Singles at the 1st Teqball National Championship, then becomes the first Indian to win an international Teqball match (Rank 5) at the 1st Asian-Pacific Teqball Cup, China.
2021
Vinit Jain founds Teqball Mumbai and wins Gold in Men's Doubles at the 1st Teqball Beach National Championship.
2022
The club wins Gold at the Senior National Teqball Championship, Erode, and competes internationally at the Teqball World Series (Paris, Poland) and World Championship (Germany).
2023
Teqball Mumbai's busiest international year: tours through Dubai, Spain, Thailand and Vietnam, alongside a National Championship title in Nashik.
2024
Vinit Jain wins Gold at the National Championship, Mumbai, and the squad competes at the Teqball World Championship, Vietnam.
2025
Atharva Sakpal wins Gold at the National Youth Championship and represents India at the Asian Youth Games, Bahrain (9th, Men's Singles), with Vinit Jain as Team India Coach.
2026
Mumbai Teq League Season 7 concludes with 48 players, and Vinit Jain tops the Men's Singles Asian Games Selection Trials in Nashik.
Needs confirmation: India's final Asian Games 2026 squad for Aichi–Nagoya, Japan

The Beginning

Before teqball, Vinit Jain was already a multi-sport athlete: leading India's U-21 team at the Minifootball World Cup in Prague (2018), and winning Bronze at both the Minifootball National Championship (2018) and the Futsal National Championship (2019).

The Athlete

Before Teqball Mumbai existed, Vinit Jain was already India's top competitor, winning Gold in Men's Singles at the 1st Teqball National Championship in 2019.

Representing India

That same year, he became the first Indian to win an international Teqball match, finishing Rank 5 at the 1st Asian-Pacific Teqball Cup in China.

Building Teqball Mumbai

In 2021, Vinit founded Teqball Mumbai, and won Gold in Men's Doubles at the 1st Teqball Beach National Championship that same year. Over the seasons that followed, he took the club's athletes across three continents: World Series events in Paris, Poland and Vietnam; World Championships in Germany and Thailand; and national titles in Erode, Nashik and Mumbai, all while continuing to compete himself, winning Gold in Men's Singles at both the 2023 and 2024 National Championships.

The Vision for India

SAMPLE COPY: Vinit's vision for Indian teqball, in his own words.

The Next Chapter

In 2025, Vinit stepped into a new role as Team India Coach at the Asian Youth Games in Bahrain, guiding Teqball Mumbai's Atharva Sakpal to a 9th-place finish on the international stage. In 2026, he topped the Men's Singles Asian Games Selection Trials in Nashik. Whether that puts him on the plane to the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi–Nagoya, Japan, as coach, athlete, or both, needs confirmation from Teqball Mumbai.

Build the future of Indian teqball with us

What is Teqball

A football-based sport played on a specially curved table, explained in under 60 seconds.

How do you play

Two players or pairs use football touches (no hands) to return the ball across a curved table, scoring points like table tennis.

Why footballers play it

  • Ball control
  • First touch
  • Coordination
  • Concentration
  • Decision-making
  • Technical development

Who can play

Beginners through elite athletes, the table adapts the game to every level, with no age or gender restrictions.

Where it comes from

The idea was born in Hungary in 2012, when former footballer Gábor Borsányi began experimenting with a curved table-tennis table to keep the ball bouncing back to his feet. Working with computer scientist Viktor Huszár, the first teqball table was built in 2014. Brazilian football legend Ronaldinho officially unveiled the sport in Budapest in 2016 and remains one of its global ambassadors.

The table

3 m long and 1.7 m wide, arching up to 0.76 m at its peak where the net divides the two sides. Played with a standard size-5 football, kept at a lower pressure than a normal match ball.

On the global stage

Recognised by the Olympic Council of Asia (2018) and the Association of National Olympic Committees of Africa (2019), and a full member of the Global Association of International Sports Federations (2020). Teqball has featured at the Asian Beach Games, the European Games, and (as of 2025) the Asian Youth Games, and is now pursuing full Olympic recognition.

Watch Teqball
  • Played with a standard football: size 5 is official.
  • Singles (1v1) or doubles (2v2).
  • Matches are best-of-three sets, each played to 12 points.
  • Each serve gets two attempts to land legally; serve rotates every four points.
  • No player may touch the ball twice in a row with the same body part, or return it twice in a row with the same body part.
  • Each side gets up to three touches to send the ball back, with no hands or arms.
  • In doubles, both partners must touch the ball before it crosses back over.
  • Touching the table, or reaching into the opponent's side, isn't allowed.
  • A ball that catches the table's edge is replayed, not scored.
